chunks: "Serpentining a diff pair means adding a little extra length to the shorter trace so that the two halves arrive together.
It's important because any skew within the pair turns some of the differential signal into common-mode, which hurts the eye and radiates.
At 6 picoseconds per millimetre, a single 90 degree bend with typical spacing makes the outer trace about 0.
7 millimetres longer, and that is already around 4 picoseconds, a few percent of a bit at 10 gigabit.
So the technique is: right after each bend, or wherever the traces diverge, I add a small jog or accordion on the shorter, inner trace to give it back that length.
I keep it local because the common-mode noise is generated along the section where the lengths differ, so fixing it at the far end doesn't fix the middle.

The jog is small with 45 degree or curved corners, and I keep the legs apart by at least three or four trace widths so they don't couple with each other, and I try not to pull the trace far from its partner, since that raises the differential impedance.

If the whole pair needs more length, to match another pair or a clock, I meander the pair together, as a coupled pair with symmetric bends, so both traces gain the same length instead of adding it to just one."
